title: Analyte monitoring device and methods of use

report.headline: Dead patent with a future: this expired Abbott glucose-sensor patent scores 90/100 (high confidence) because the field is busy and growing, but it sits inside one of the most crowded, regulated and patent-dense markets in medical devices.
report.what_it_is: It describes a small sensor worn on the skin, with a tip under the skin that measures a substance in body fluid, such as glucose, and a transmitter that sends the reading wirelessly to a display unit. It also covers linking that sensor to a drug-delivery device, such as an insulin pump, so the drug dose can respond to the readings.

why_it_died.text: It did not die early. It ran its full term and ended on 2021-04-09. The owner paid every maintenance fee, which suggests Abbott valued it to the end. That is why the 'died for money, not merit' signal scores only half marks (7.5/15): there was no abandonment signal, only natural expiry.

case_for.point: The field is clearly alive. Abbott sells a product in this space today, the FreeStyle Libre 3 Plus, through US pharmacies. This drives the full 30/30 'field still alive' score.

Momentum is recent and comes from outside Abbott. 35 citing filings date from 2019 on. 13 filings by unrelated owners were filed after the patent expired. Insulet alone has 17 filings building on it since 2019.
It was a foundational patent. 849 later filings cite it, and examiners used it against 208 later applications. That suggests the basic idea is well understood and widely referenced.
The claims were broad at grant. The shortest independent claim is 84 words across 64 claims, and the family was filed in 7 jurisdictions. This earned the full breadth score.

case_against.point: This is a crowded, established market, not an open gap. The original owner still sells products here, and big players like Insulet keep filing patents on top of the idea.
Abbott appears to have surrounded this patent with newer ones. It filed 164 later patents citing this one that may still be in force, including work on ketone sensors.
Lots of citations show technical relevance, not proof of revenue for a newcomer. A high score may reflect how busy the field is, not how easy it is to enter.

blockers.point: Newer patents may cover the parts that make a modern product work. That includes 164 later Abbott filings and 108 patents by other owners. Expiry of this one patent may not mean the space is clear. This is worth checking with an attorney.

FDA clearance is likely needed before you can sell. An implanted or skin-worn sensor may need 510(k), De Novo or PMA, and higher-risk classes need clinical data. That can mean years and serious money.
Wireless links bring standards and licensing issues. Radios need FCC authorization, and standards like 802.11 are covered by many live standard-essential patents.
The patent shows the idea, not how to manufacture it. Making reliable implantable electrodes at scale is know-how you would have to rebuild yourself.

assumption_to_test.assumption: There is a specific group of users or buyers whose needs current sensors like the FreeStyle Libre do not meet, and who would switch to or pay for a new entrant's sensor.
assumption_to_test.why_riskiest: The incumbent still sells a product built on this idea, and other big companies keep filing on top of it. Without a clear underserved niche, a startup would face the incumbents plus long regulatory costs with no reason for customers to switch.
assumption_to_test.how_to_test: In two weeks, interview 15-20 current CGM users, diabetes educators or clinic buyers. Recruit through online diabetes communities, at a cost under $300 in gift cards. Ask what they dislike about their current sensor, what they pay, and what would make them switch. Also run a $150 landing page aimed at one niche, such as ketone monitoring, veterinary use or uninsured users, and measure sign-up rate. Kill or pivot if fewer than about a third of interviewees name the same unmet need.

attorney_questions: Which of Abbott's 164 later citing filings, and the 108 examiner-cited patents from other owners, appear most likely to cover a modern skin-worn sensor with wireless transmission, and what would a freedom-to-operate search cost?
Does the expiry of US6560471B1 on 2021-04-09 affect anything in the 7 other jurisdictions where the family was filed, or should we check each one separately?
If we target a narrower use, such as non-glucose analytes or non-medical uses, how might that change both the patent risk and the FDA pathway?
report.disclaimer: Research and triage only, not legal advice. This report is not a patentability, validity or freedom-to-operate opinion. Patent status shown here comes from public records that can lag or be wrong. An expired patent is not the same as free to use: follow-on patents, regulatory exclusivity, trade secrets and standards can still block a product. Confirm with a registered patent attorney before acting.

signals.signal: The field is still technically active long after filing. The patent is heavily cited, and examiners keep using it as prior art against new applications.
Interest continued near and after the end of term. Unrelated owners kept building on this work, including filings with priority dates after the 2021 expiry.
Recent citing activity is concentrated in one company. Insulet accounts for most post-2019 citing filings, which suggests interest in pairing sensors with drug delivery, as the abstract describes.

Products in this category are on the market today. Abbott's FreeStyle Libre 3 Plus is sold through retail pharmacy and DME channels, although the evidence does not tie that product to this specific patent.

read.who_is_active: Insulet Corporation has the most recent citing filings (17 since 2019), with single filings from Informed Data Systems, Heraeus Medical, Alimetry and National Yunlin University of Science and Technology. Abbott sells a continuous glucose sensor product in this category.
read.market_read: On-body electrochemical analyte monitoring with wireless display remains an active, commercialized field with continuing patent activity, especially around linking sensors to drug delivery. Citation counts show technical relevance rather than revenue, so a founder should treat this as evidence of a crowded, established space and consult a patent attorney before relying on any freedom-to-operate assumptions.
